finalText:
**Merge** creates a new commit that combines two branches, keeping their full history. The graph shows both branches existed and when they converged.

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of the target branch, rewriting history to make it linear. It's as if you developed sequentially instead of in parallel.

**Tradeoff:**
- Merge: Preserves complete history, safe for public branches (never rewrites what others have)
- Rebase: Cleaner, linear history and easier to read, but rewrites history (so only use on branches you own or haven't pushed)

**When to reach for each:**

| Situation | Use |
|-----------|-----|
| Feature branch, not yet pushed | **Rebase** before pushing to keep the main branch history clean |
| Feature branch others pulled from | **Merge** — you'd break their history by rebasing |
| Public/shared branch (main, release) | **Merge** — never rebase public history |
| Syncing your branch with upstream changes | **Rebase** locally to get a linear view; **merge** if others use your branch |
| Pull request workflow | **Rebase** during development (locally), **merge** when integrating (often automatic via GitHub/GitLab) |

**The rule of thumb:** Rebase is "cleaning up your desk before you leave," merge is "showing your work as it happened." Once work is shared, don't rebase — the history is already there.
